extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and general readers interested in humor theory (psychology, linguistics, philosophy, comedy studies)
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic survey of major academic and philosophical theories that attempt to explain what makes things humorous, including mechanisms, examples, and empirical or historical support. Useful for analyzing, classifying, or producing humor from multiple disciplinary perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relief theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is a mechanism for releasing pent-up emotions or tension; laughter reduces psychological stress and serves as a homeostatic release of excess nervous/psychic energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains laughter as easing fear or social inhibitions (e.g., tickling). Historical proponents include Spencer, Freud, Kant; used as a dramatic/comedic device (comic relief). Distinguishes tendentious vs non-tendentious humor (Freud). Empirical studies (e.g., Zillmann & Bryant) support that release/innocuous cues amplify amusement. Use cases: jokes that relieve guilt or tension. Anti-patterns: humor that lacks innocuous elements when hostility is present may not be socially acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority theory
rubrics_metrics.description: People laugh because they feel superior to others — laughter expresses a sudden sense of glory or superiority at another's misfortune, infirmity, or failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rooted in Hobbes, Plato, Aristotle; explains jokes based on ridicule, physical defects, slips. Hobbes lists typical triggers (unexpected success beyond expectations, perception of defects, absurdity). Interacts with incongruity and aggression in many jokes. Criticisms note many humorous instances lack superiority elements; feelings of superiority may be distinct from humor itself. Practical implication: jokes that ‘punch down’ risk ethical issues; punching up is seen as more acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affective disposition theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience moral judgments and dispositions toward characters determine amusement: people enjoy when desired outcomes happen to liked characters or misfortune befalls disliked characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies how disposition toward victim and victor modulate mirth: stronger negative disposition toward victim increases mirth; positive disposition toward victim decreases mirth, etc. Applied especially to media and entertainment. Explains why identical events produce differing humor responses depending on audience sympathy and moral evaluation. Links to ethical norms (punching up/down).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor arises from incongruity — a perception contrary to expectation, often resolved to produce amusement (incongruity-resolution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common in wordplay and riddle jokes: setup produces expectation, punchline produces cognitive dissonance then resolution. Historical proponents include Hutcheson, Kant, Schopenhauer, Bergson. Variants emphasize sudden shift in perspective, structure mapping, or collision of frames. Use cases: puns, perspective-shift jokes, surprises. Note overlap with relief/superiority theories in many instances; degree and type of incongruity affect visceral vs appreciative responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benign violation theory (BVT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor occurs when a situation simultaneously constitutes a violation of how the world 'ought to be' and is perceived as benign; the perceiver must see both the violation and its benignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three conditions: something threatens a norm; it seems benign; the person perceives both interpretations. Examples: tickling, play-fighting, risqué jokes. Benignity can arise from alternative norms, psychological distance, or weak commitment to the norm. Predicts individual/context differences in amusement (e.g., churchgoers less amused by sacred-norm violations). Useful for explaining moral/ethical humor sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script-based semantic theory of humor (SSTH)
rubrics_metrics.description: A linguistic theory (for verbal jokes) that explains humor by compatibility of a text with two opposing semantic 'scripts'; the punchline triggers an abrupt switch from the primary script to the opposing script.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires (i) text compatible with two scripts and (ii) the scripts are opposite. Example: 'Is the doctor at home?' joke with DOCTOR and LOVER scripts. Offers categories of script opposition (actual/non-actual, good/bad, obscene/non-obscene, life/death, etc.). Cultural dependence: scripts and oppositions vary by culture. Anti-pattern: mere juxtaposition of incongruous elements without a clever way to make them pseudo-sense together will not produce a joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Theory of Verbal Humor (GTVH)
rubrics_metrics.description: An extension of SSTH that models verbal jokes using six independent Knowledge Resources (KRs) to represent and compare jokes systematically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrates Script Opposition into a hierarchical model. Advantages: can categorize all humorous texts (not only short jokes) and measure similarity between jokes by KR overlap. Ordering of KRs is debated; empirical tests partially successful. Example application: variants of 'light bulb' jokes shifted by one KR each. Use as an analytic framework for joke generation and classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: GTVH — Script opposition (SO)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of GTVH's Knowledge Resources: the oppositional script pair (e.g., real/unreal, good/bad) that underlies the joke's semantic tension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary KR that constrains lower-level choices (e.g., target selection). Determines high-level theme of the joke and limits which targets/narrative strategies are plausible for a given opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: GTVH — Logical mechanism (LM)
rubrics_metrics.description: GTVH KR describing the mechanism that connects the different scripts in the joke (e.g., pun, faulty logic, false analogy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies the technical device that effects the shift between scripts. LM choices influence the cognitive processing required and the type of comedic payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: GTVH — Situation (SI)
rubrics_metrics.description: GTVH KR that includes objects, activities, instruments, or props needed to tell the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies situational elements that instantiate the scripts and make the joke tellable; changes in SI can alter joke plausibility and audience uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: GTVH — Target (TA)
rubrics_metrics.description: GTVH KR identifying the actor(s) who become the butt of the joke; an optional labeling that shapes stereotypes and social meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target selection is culturally inflected and can determine offense potential; TA is constrained by SO and affects ethical/social reading of the joke (punching up/down considerations).

rubrics_metrics.name: GTVH — Narrative strategy (NS)
rubrics_metrics.description: GTVH KR addressing the joke's narrative format (simple narrative, dialogue, riddle, etc.) and how the joke is structured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NS determines genre/subgenre of the humorous text and, together with LM and LA, shapes timing and delivery possibilities. Attardo expanded NS to include longer oral/printed narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: GTVH — Language (LA)
rubrics_metrics.description: GTVH KR containing all linguistic information necessary for verbalization: exact wording and placement of functional elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LA controls phrasing, word choice, and surface realization; two jokes with identical KRs may differ in funniness by LA differences (intonation, lexical choices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer model of humor (Suslov)
rubrics_metrics.description: A computational/biological model positing a malfunction in information processing where a false hypothesis is rapidly deleted, producing an incongruity-resolution effect plus timing considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adds timing and neural-network realizations to incongruity-resolution; explains differences in susceptibility, intonation effects, nervous laughter, and tickling. Argues humor has biological origins while social functions arose later. Suggests practical realization would require large databases for automatic humor systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misattribution theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences sometimes cannot identify precisely what causes amusement and misattribute their laughter to innocuous elements while hostility/taboo elements are the real drivers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from Freud and formalized by Zillmann & Bryant for tendentious humor; explains why people claim to laugh at innocent wordplay while unconscious hostility produces the laugh. Implication: analyzing what audiences say they find funny can be misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ontic-epistemic theory of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter responds to a cognitive impasse where social reality appears not factual — the comic arises when social/normative perceptions lose factual status, producing a reset of social perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marteinson's theory uses notions like Deculturation and Relativisation to explain comic perception; laughter anesthetizes the mind and communicates the humorous reaction socially. Applies to cases where social reality conflicts with factual reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual selection theory (humor as mate signal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor evolved by sexual selection as an indicator of desirable traits (e.g., intelligence); humor signals fitness rather than directly aiding survival.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geoffrey Miller argues humor had limited direct survival value on the savanna but emerged as a sexual-display trait. Implication: comedic ability may correlate with cognitive capacities valued in mate choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection of mistaken reasoning (Hurley, Dennett, Adams)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor evolved to strengthen the brain's ability to detect mistaken reasoning and thus improve practical problem solving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames humor as adaptive cognitive training for finding errors in belief structures; consistent with sexual-selection arguments but emphasizes survival/reasoning advantages of humor-related cognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as defense mechanism (Vaillant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychodynamic account that classifies humor as a mature defense mechanism (level 4): overt expression of unpleasant ideas/feelings in a way that gives pleasure to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts humor (level 4) with wit (level 3 displacement). Use: reframing distressing topics into humorous form to manage emotion. Limits: may skirt seriousness rather than resolve underlying distress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense of humor vs sense of seriousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to distinguish when something should be taken literally or not; important when humor conveys a serious point or risks crossing into bad taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychological and social factors determine whether humor is interpreted as serious or not (e.g., court jesters vs. offensive jokes). Beware that jokes intended as frivolous can be taken seriously if context or delivery fails; bad-taste humor can cross lines and be interpreted as non-humorous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor, metonymy, and allegory in humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Cognitive-linguistic approaches emphasize the role of metaphor, metonymy, structure-mapping, and conceptual blending in producing humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tony Veale and others formalize how metaphorical mappings and conceptual blends produce novelty and comedic effects; connects to Koestler's bisociation and Gentner/Lakoff theoretical frameworks. Useful for computational modeling of humor and for crafting metaphoric jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: O'Shannon model of the comedic event
rubrics_metrics.description: A unified framework dividing comedy into context, information, aspects of awareness, and enhancers/inhibitors; explains interactional dynamics producing comedic responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context primes reception; information carries cognitive load and incongruity; awareness layers shape interpretation; enhancers/inhibitors (superiority, relief, aggression, identification, shock) modulate response. Predicts variety: high incongruity can produce visceral laughter, low-incongruity wordplay may elicit appreciative humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unnoticed fall-back to former behavior patterns model
rubrics_metrics.description: Defines laughter as an acoustic signal alerting that someone has unconsciously reverted to an old behavioral pattern; unifies superiority and incongruity explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positions ticklishness and evolutionary bipedalism as related phenomena. Useful for explaining social signaling function of laughter and some forms of comedic detection of behavioral slips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bergson's theory (mechanism applied to life / rigidity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy arises from perceiving mechanical rigidity or automatism applied to living, flexible life; laughter serves social/moral function to correct eccentric or rigid behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bergson emphasizes movement, elasticity vs. rigidity; comic situations show inflexibility (falls, absent-mindedness, repetitive gestures). Laughter is an intellectual, not emotional, response and functions as social corrective. Use: physical/comic acting that emphasizes mechanical repetition or rigidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex systems theory applied to humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying complexity/chaos theory to humor to account for how interacting parts of a discourse/community produce emergent humorous phenomena over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calls for transdisciplinary work; applications include modeling incongruity-resolution dynamics and conversational humor emergence (memes, running jokes). Useful for studying emergent patterns and time-dependent dynamics of humor rather than single-joke mechanisms.
